lead: Isaac is born and weaned, and Sarah demands that Hagar and her son be sent away. Abraham, distressed, obeys God and sends them into the wilderness of Beer-sheba. When the water runs out and Hagar cannot bear to watch the child die, God hears the voice of the boy and opens her eyes to a well. In the Gospel Jesus crosses to Gentile land, delivers two men possessed by demons, and the townspeople, instead of rejoicing, ask him to leave. Psalm 34 answers both: “The Lord hears the cry of the poor.” Today the Church may remember the first martyrs of the Church of Rome.

r.h: God has heard the voice of the boy
set: The promise has been fulfilled: Isaac is born when Abraham is a hundred. At the feast of his weaning, Sarah sees Ishmael, the son of Hagar the Egyptian slave woman, “playing” with Isaac, and fears for her son’s inheritance. The story is painful and honest. Scripture does not hide the jealousy and harshness in the family of the patriarchs.

Hagar had once run away into the wilderness before Ishmael’s birth, and the angel had met her there and named the child “God hears” (16:7–14). Now she is in the wilderness again, sent away, and God hears once more.
str: vv. 5, 8: Isaac born; the feast of his weaning.
vv. 9–10: Sarah demands that Hagar and her son be cast out.
vv. 11–13: Abraham is distressed; God tells him to listen, and promises that Ishmael too will be a nation.
vv. 14–16: bread and a skin of water; the wilderness; Hagar weeps at a bowshot’s distance.
vv. 17–20a: God hears; the angel calls; the well; God is with the boy.
kw: The text never names Ishmael in this passage; he is “the boy”, “the child”, “your offspring”. But the story keeps saying that God “heard”, the meaning of his name.
“God heard the voice of the boy” (v. 17). In Scripture God hears the cry of the weak, as he heard Israel in Egypt (Exodus 3:7).
Water in the desert means life. God opens Hagar’s eyes to see what was already there.
vv: The matter was very distressing to Abraham on account of his son.
Abraham loves Ishmael. The father of faith is not shown as cold; he suffers.
As for the son of the slave woman, I will make a nation of him also, because he is your offspring.
God’s promise reaches beyond the line of the covenant. Ishmael is not abandoned.
And God heard the voice of the boy;
Hagar wept, but it is the boy’s voice that God hears. The angel says “Do not be afraid”, as angels so often do in Scripture.
Then God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water.
Despair had hidden the well from her. God’s help often comes as the opening of our eyes.
ch: St Paul uses Hagar and Sarah in an allegory about slavery and sonship in Galatians 4:21–31. That allegory concerns living by grace, not a verdict on any people, and the Church is careful never to use it against the Jewish people, to whom “belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants” (Romans 9:4; CCC 839). The Second Vatican Council notes that Muslims link their faith with Abraham, and asks Christians and Muslims to forget past quarrels and work together for justice and peace (Nostra Aetate 3). Psalm 34 gives the Church’s reading of today’s story: the Lord hears the cry of the poor, of the outcast mother and the thirsty child.

r.h: They begged him to leave their neighbourhood
set: Jesus has just calmed the storm on the lake (8:23–27). He lands on the eastern shore, in the region of the Decapolis, mostly Gentile country, where pigs were kept. Mark and Luke tell the same story with one man; Matthew has two, as he does elsewhere (compare 20:30). The place name differs in the manuscripts: Gadarenes, Gerasenes or Gergesenes.
str: v. 28: two fierce demoniacs come out of the tombs.
v. 29: “What have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?”
vv. 30–32: the demons beg to enter the swine; “Go!”; the herd rushes into the sea.
vv. 33–34: the swineherds tell the town; the townspeople ask Jesus to leave.
kw: People under the power of evil spirits. They live among the tombs, the place of death, and no one can pass that way.
The demons know that a time of judgment is coming when their power will end. In Jesus that end has already begun.
The same verb is used of the demons begging (v. 31) and of the townspeople begging Jesus to leave (v. 34). Both want him at a distance.
vv: What have you to do with us, Son of God?
The demons recognise who Jesus is before the disciples fully do. Knowing is not the same as believing (compare James 2:19).
One word is enough. Jesus does not struggle with the demons; he commands them.
when they saw him, they begged him to leave their neighborhood.
They count the loss of the pigs and are afraid. The healing of two men matters less to them than their property and their quiet.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ exorcisms release people from the domination of demons and anticipate his great victory over “the ruler of this world” (CCC 550). The Church continues this ministry: in baptism she prays for deliverance from evil, and in grave cases a priest authorised by the bishop may perform a solemn exorcism (CCC 1673). The Gospel also asks a hard question: do I prefer my comfort, my possessions or my routine to the presence of Christ who changes things?

rite: Today the Church may keep the memorial of the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church. After the great fire of Rome in the year 64, the emperor Nero blamed the Christians, and the Roman historian Tacitus records that a vast multitude were put to death with cruel tortures. St Clement of Rome later spoke of “a great multitude of the elect” who suffered there (in substance). They are remembered on the day after Saints Peter and Paul, who died in the same persecution. Their names are unknown, but like Hagar’s child, their cry was heard by God. Christians in many lands still suffer for their faith; we pray for them, and for those who wrong them.
study: When have I, like Hagar, been unable to see the “well” God had placed near me? Who helped open my eyes?
Is there any part of my life where I have quietly asked Jesus to “leave”, because his presence would cost me something?
